title: Restructure goals: Identifying organizational gaps
text: Hello, I am Muskin Agrawal and this video is a summary of week three of the Humanitarian's AI website restructure. A stakeholder insight plan, a full set of discussion questions, and the beginnings of a structural hierarchy strategy for the home page. Two weeks of

title: Mapping eight competing target audiences
text: Auditing produced a specification, a type scale, a contrast target, a line length. Every one of those is a decision design can make on its own. This week is about the decisions it cannot. A measurement can tell you the hero is media heavy. It cannot tell you who the site is for. That is not a design

title: Core contradictions: Donation transparency & language barriers
text: Question. It belongs to the organization. The week started by counting who the home page is for. It speaks to eight different audiences, fellows and international graduates, donors, mentors, educators, partner organizations, children and families, volunteers, and the general public. Eight audiences, one page, no stated order of priority. Then the vocabulary.

title: Stakeholder Discussion Guide: Open questions on trust
text: The home page runs about 1,200 words and carries 24 named concepts a first-time reader has to decode. Tier one, tiers three to six, irreducibly human, botspeak, atoms. Roughly one piece of internal shorthand every 50 words. And the exits. 13 separate learn more and explore links leave the home page. 13 equally weighted onward paths is 13 ways to leave and no way to be led. The

title: Structuring homepage hierarchy: Leading with search intent
text: Same page makes three asks at once, side by side and identically weighted. Donate now, volunteer, watch on YouTube. Which of those matters most is not a question a designer can answer. For a donor, the trust picture is mixed. The site states its 501c3 status and its EIN. It does not publish an annual report, a form 990, a named board, or a

title: Next steps & week 4 overview
text: Third-party charity rating. And one finding needs an answer before any of it gets designed. The home page says 100% of donations fund the programs, mentorship, and project support. The footer of the same page says 100% of all donations support direct operational costs, including legal fees and staff salaries. Both cannot be the promise. Success metrics are the other gap. Every number on the home page is a tier label, a legal identifier, a chapter count, or a copyright year. Not one of them is an outcome. No fellows placed, no tools delivered. None of those are design decisions. Every one of them is an organizational decision that a designer can surface, but should not make alone. So, the next step is to ask. The output of this week is a discussion guide, a

Structured set of open questions for stakeholders, mentors, and donors across eight themes: audience priority, first impression, primary action, terminology, navigation, tone, trust, and success metrics. On audience and message, if a first-time visitor reads one sentence and leaves, what should that sentence have told them? Which single audience matters most this quarter? And what do people most often misunderstand about what this organization does? On action and language, if a visitor does exactly one thing, what should it be? Which of these named concepts would you keep if a stranger had to understand without help? And which navigation links exist because someone still needs them? On trust and proof, what would a donor need to see to give with confidence? What is the one number that would show this year was worth funding? And

Where should the writing sound like a research group and where like a program a family could join? Alongside the questions, the structural hierarchy strategy took shape. The principle is the one the audit kept pointing at. Lead with what a visitor came looking for and let what the organization offers follow from that. That hierarchy work fed one more round of hero refinement. It stays a direction, not a layout, deliberately. The hero should not be redrawn until the people who own the message have said which message leads. Week one was the audit. Week two was the specification. Week three is the questions and the meeting they are for. Week four moves to navigation cleanup with the developer and to agreeing how design and development hand work over. Humanitarians.data.i restructure, week three of four.
